title: Être fort pour être utile: the Naval Officer, the Ruins of Saint-Pierre, and the Method Made Outdoors
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Borda and the Atlantic Circuit

stops.name: Paris, born in the fifth arrondissement
stops.date_confidence: Attested. Date and arrondissement agree across fr.wikipedia and en.wikipedia. No street address or birth house was located, so the coordinate is the general centre of the 5th arrondissement rather than a building.
stops.campa: In the fifth arrondissement, within walking distance of the Jardin des Plantes and its anatomy halls, a son is born to a Paris household on the twenty-seventh of April 1875. He is named Georges. The Third Republic is five years old and still counting the dead of Sedan, and the argument over why French bodies lost that war, and what school gymnastics ought to do about it, is already running through the ministries. It will run for the whole of his life. After the date and the arrondissement, the record holds nothing about him until 1893.
suggested_refs: The post-1870 French debate on national physical regeneration, the standing context of his entire career

stops.name: Brest, the École navale aboard the Borda
stops.date_confidence: Year attested (en.wikipedia, '1893: Entered École navale'); month and day unknown and defaulted to 01-01. That the school's seat in this period was the hulk Borda in the Brest roadstead is general naval history, not confirmed for Hébert's own case in this research: treat the Borda and Brest specificity as reconstruction.
stops.campa: At eighteen he enters the École navale, whose whole establishment in these years is a dismasted ship of the line, the Borda, moored in the roadstead at Brest. Dormitories on the gun decks, classrooms below, the sea outside the ports. Cadets take navigation, gunnery, and the physical drill of the period: Swedish stiffness and apparatus gymnastics, performed in ranks, under a roof, to a whistle. He will spend fifty years arguing that the drill itself is the error. For now he is a cadet on a hulk, and he finishes sixtieth of seventy-two.
suggested_refs: The Borda school-hulk at Brest, seat of the École navale until 1913

stops.name: Cherbourg, made aspirant
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day by fr.wikipedia ('aspirant à Cherbourg', 5 October 1896). The graduation rank of 60th of 72 comes from en.wikipedia. fr.wikipedia places him aboard the cruiser Dubourdieu in 1897, not 1896; the enseigne de vaisseau promotion of 5 October 1898 is given without a place.
stops.campa: On the fifth of October 1896 he is made aspirant at Cherbourg, and the following year takes his post aboard the cruiser Dubourdieu. Two years after that, again on a fifth of October, he is promoted enseigne de vaisseau. The career is unremarkable and the postings are unremarkable: watch-keeping, coaling, the long boredom of a peacetime navy that has not fought a fleet action in living memory. What is not unremarkable is what he does with the ports. He goes ashore and watches how people move.
suggested_refs: The cruiser Dubourdieu, his first ship as aspirant

stops.name: Fort-de-France, the Atlantic circuit and the bodies ashore
stops.date_confidence: Composite stop, not a single verified landmark. en.wikipedia gives only 'travels to South America, West Indies, and North America until 1903' with no ports and no dates. Date defaulted to the middle of that range; coordinate placed at Martinique as the best-documented endpoint of the cruising period.
stops.campa: From the late 1890s he sails the Atlantic circuit the French navy keeps: South America, the West Indies, North America, in ships still carrying sail. At each landfall he watches bodies that have never entered a gymnasium, dockers and fishermen and villagers, and finds them faster and more durable than the drilled crews he serves with. It is an officer's colonial gaze and he never once examines it as such. The conclusion he draws from it, and keeps for fifty years, is that the apparatus in the gymnasium is not what makes a body strong.
stops.quote: Their bodies were splendid, flexible, nimble, skillful, enduring, resistant and yet they had no other tutor in gymnastics but their lives in nature.
stops.quote_source: Hébert, as rendered in English by Christopher McDougall, Natural Born Heroes (2016), p. 228; no French primary text for the sentence was located, and archive.org's copy of McDougall is lending-restricted, so p. 228 is Wikipedia's citation, unverified at first hand.
suggested_refs: The colonial-primitivist strand in European physical culture around 1900, of which this observation is a specimen
sources: Christopher McDougall, Natural Born Heroes (2016), p. 228, cited via en.wikipedia

stops.name: Saint-Pierre, ashore in the burned city
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day. The sources contradict each other on his ship: fr.wikipedia puts him aboard the D'Estrées, en.wikipedia aboard the Suchet, and the contemporary Tour du monde account names 'l'enseigne de vaisseau Hébert, du Suchet'. Independent weight favours the Suchet, which en.wikipedia's own article on that cruiser documents off Saint-Pierre from 6 May. The contradiction is recorded, not resolved.
stops.campa: Mont Pelée opens on the morning of the eighth of May and Saint-Pierre, a city of some twenty-eight thousand people, ceases to exist inside a few minutes. A cruiser closes the shore through falling ash and lowers a boat. Hébert, enseigne de vaisseau, twenty-seven years old, goes in it. What the shore party finds in the streets is not a rescue operation. It is carbonized stone, and the shapes of people standing where they stood. They walk in as far as the heat allows and find nobody to take off.
stops.quote: Je demande au capitaine de s'approcher le plus près possible de Saint-Pierre et, faisant mettre un canot à la mer, nous nous dirigeons vers la ville même, le lieutenant, l'enseigne (l'enseigne de vaisseau Hébert, du Suchet) et moi.
stops.quote_source: 'La Catastrophe de la Martinique', Le Tour du monde, nouvelle série, 8e année (1902), Paris, Hachette, p. 412, transcribed on French Wikisource. The page does not name its narrator; the common identification of him as a magistrate is not supported by the page itself.
suggested_refs: The 1902 eruption of Mount Pelée and the naval relief operation out of Fort-de-France
sources: fr.wikisource, Le Tour du monde, nouvelle série, vol. 8, p. 412

stops.name: The coast toward Le Carbet, sailors taken off the rocks
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The detail comes from the dossier's description of a contemporary account in Le Tour du monde that could not be independently retrieved at this specific point in the research; it is a checkable claim rather than vague tradition, and is kept flagged rather than dropped.
stops.campa: Along the coast south of the dead city, boats from the cruiser work the rocks. A group of sailors is found clinging there, alive, blistered, and taken off. Set against twenty-eight thousand dead it is almost nothing, and it is also the only thing anyone afloat that morning can actually do: bring a boat in close, take hands, pull. He is twenty-seven years old, in a boat, under ash, doing the one useful thing on offer. The number taken off is small and the report of it is short.
suggested_refs: The coastal strip between Saint-Pierre and Le Carbet, worked by ships' boats on 8 May 1902
sources: Le Tour du monde (1902), as described in the research dossier; not independently retrieved

stops.name: Fort-de-France, the seven hundred
stops.date_confidence: The figure of 700 is stated as fact by both fr.wikipedia ('participera au secours de 700 personnes') and en.wikipedia, so it is not merely movement tradition. It is also within documented scale: en.wikipedia's 'French cruiser Suchet' records around 1,200 people landed at Fort-de-France by 11 May. What is unverified is Hébert's personal leadership of that rescue, not the number. Date is the documented completion of the evacuation.
stops.campa: The Suchet runs survivors down the coast to Fort-de-France through the week; by the eleventh of May roughly twelve hundred people have been landed there. Seven hundred of them are afterwards credited to Hébert personally, in encyclopedias and in the movement that takes his name, as a rescue he led. The naval operation is real and the order of magnitude is documented. The single officer at the head of it is not. He dates his own vocation from these days, and says so once, flatly, in a wartime book written thirteen years later.
stops.quote: Dès lors ma voie était tracée. Dans notre société pacifique et pervertie, peut-être par excès de civilisation, il fallait recréer des êtres forts.
stops.quote_source: Georges Hébert, La Culture virile et les devoirs de l'officier combattant, as quoted with this attribution on entrainement-naturel.org; the primary edition was not opened, so the wording is reported rather than collated.
suggested_refs: en.wikipedia, 'French cruiser Suchet', for the documented scale of the naval evacuation

segments.name: Lorient: the Method Made on Broken Ground

stops.name: Lorient, the fusiliers marins and the ten families of movement
stops.date_confidence: Year attested by both wikis, which converge on Lorient as the method's laboratory; sources vary between 1903 and 1904 for the start, and month and day are unknown and defaulted. The running total of roughly 1,000 men through 1912 is en.wikipedia's.
stops.campa: Posted to the marine fusiliers at Lorient, he is given men, ground, and an instruction to make them fit. He takes them outside. The training is walking, running, jumping, quadrupedal movement, climbing, balancing, throwing, lifting, defending, and swimming: ten families of movement, worked over broken country in whatever weather the day supplies, using no apparatus that a wood does not already contain. Roughly a thousand men pass through it by 1912. The motto he fixes to the whole undertaking is four words long.
stops.quote_source: Hébert's motto, quoted universally in the secondary and institutional literature; no dated primary edition, page, or first utterance was located for it.
suggested_refs: The École du Bataillon des fusiliers marins at Lorient, where the méthode naturelle was built

stops.name: Paris, the ring at the Cirque Molier
stops.date_confidence: Venue attested and located: fr.wikipedia, 'Ernest Molier', gives 6 bis rue Bénouville, Paris 16e, built 1879, operating 1880 to 1933, performers exclusively aristocratic amateurs. Hébert's participation is a dossier-only claim; the Molier article names only Molier and his wife Blanche Allarty and does not mention him. Year is the dossier's; month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: Off the rue Bénouville in the sixteenth arrondissement, Ernest Molier keeps a private circus in a ring built beside his own house, where titled amateurs perform for an invited audience and no ticket is ever sold. It runs from 1880 to 1933. Hébert is said to have worked there on the bar, a naval officer among barons, testing on a trapeze the same proposition he is testing on conscripts in Brittany. Molier's own record names his wife and himself and nobody else. The story survives without a document under it.
suggested_refs: fr.wikipedia, 'Ernest Molier', on the private circus at 6 bis rue Bénouville

stops.name: Paris, L'Éducation physique raisonnée
stops.date_confidence: Corrected date. The dossier gave 1905 and claimed the French Wikipedia bibliography corroborated it; that bibliography in fact lists the book as 1907 (Paris, Vuibert et Nony). 1907 is used here. Month and day unknown and defaulted. Coordinate is the central Paris placeholder; no publisher address was pinned.
stops.campa: Vuibert et Nony bring out L'Éducation physique raisonnée, his first book, and its argument is not about exercises. It is about ends. Physical education exists in order to produce strong beings, and a strength that is not placed at somebody else's disposal is a private ornament and nothing more. The English rendering that carries the sentence into the twentieth century is a modern translator's work, and the 1905 French scan behind it reads badly and yields none of the underlying phrases on search.
stops.quote: The final goal of physical education is to make strong beings... The true Natural Method, in its broadest sense, must be considered as the result of these three particular forces; it is a physical, virile and moral synthesis.
stops.quote_source: Georges Hébert and Philippe Til, The Natural Method: Functional Exercises, vol. 3, CreateSpace, 2015, ISBN 9781515227779, quoted via en.wikipedia. The ellipsis spans three intervening paragraphs, not a clause. A modern translator's English, not collated against Hébert's French.
suggested_refs: Philippe Til's English translations of the méthode naturelle manuals

stops.name: Lorient, eight hundred apprentices measured
stops.date_confidence: Year attested by en.wikipedia ('1908: Tested method on about 800 adolescent apprentices aged 14-17'); month and day unknown and defaulted.
stops.campa: The method is turned on boys. Some eight hundred apprentices between fourteen and seventeen are put through it, and Hébert starts measuring: distance covered, height cleared, weight moved, time taken, recorded body by body and tracked across months. He is building an instrument as much as a training, a way of stating what a given boy can actually do rather than how correct he looks doing it. French physical education at this date is still mostly a matter of ranks and a whistle, and correctness is the thing it measures. The Navy reads the numbers.
suggested_refs: The apprentice cohorts at Lorient, 1908, the method's first application to adolescents

stops.name: Lorient, the Navy adopts the method
stops.date_confidence: The 1909 adoption is fr.wikipedia's and is tagged reconstruction: no decree or ministerial reference was located. The Guide pratique d'éducation physique of 1910 is attested by en.wikipedia, 'Méthode naturelle'. Month and day unknown and defaulted; the stop is pinned at Lorient rather than at a ministry.
stops.campa: In 1909 the Navy takes the méthode naturelle for its own, and the following year Hébert prints the Guide pratique d'éducation physique: the manual by which an instructor who has never met him can run a session correctly on a beach in Brittany or a parade ground in Toulon. A doctrine that began as one officer's quarrel with the drill book has become the training of a service. He has not directed a school, published his major work, or seen a war. He is thirty-four.
suggested_refs: Guide pratique d'éducation physique (1910), the method's first portable manual

stops.name: Paris, Le Code de la force
stops.date_confidence: Publication year cross-checked against the fr.wikipedia bibliography; month and day unknown and defaulted. The Chevalier de la Légion d'honneur of 1911 is attested by fr.wikipedia, section 'Reconnaissance et notoriété'. Coordinate is the central Paris placeholder.
stops.campa: Le Code de la force appears, and it is a scoring system. Twelve tests, a table, a single number for a body: run this far in this time, jump this high, lift this, swim this, and the arithmetic returns a figure comparable with any other man's figure anywhere in France. The tests are printed with their scales, so a schoolmaster can administer them without having seen the method taught. A company can now be ranked without being watched. He is made Chevalier de la Légion d'honneur the same year.
suggested_refs: Le Code de la force (1911), the twelve-test scoring table
sources: fr.wikipedia, 'Georges Hébert', bibliography and 'Reconnaissance et notoriété'

stops.name: Paris, L'Éducation physique ou l'Entraînement complet
stops.date_confidence: Year attested by the fr.wikipedia bibliography; month and day unknown and defaulted. Coordinate is the central Paris placeholder, not a located publisher's address.
stops.campa: The large book of the pre-war years, and the last thing he prints before it: complete training by the natural method, with progressions and whole sessions set out so that the ten families of movement become a curriculum anybody can pick up and run. It sells, and it is read well outside the Navy, by schoolmasters, by scout leaders, by the physical-culture press. He is thirty-seven. The photographic plates show men caught mid-movement outdoors, not posed against a studio wall.
suggested_refs: L'Éducation physique ou l'Entraînement complet par la méthode naturelle (1912)

stops.name: Paris, the International Congress of Physical Education
stops.date_confidence: Month and year attested by en.wikipedia; day unknown and defaulted. No period account of the session itself, and no venue, was located in this research, so the 'army of peace' framing is reported from the dossier and tagged reconstruction, and the coordinate is central Paris only.
stops.campa: At the International Congress of Physical Education his naval pupils give a demonstration and the press finds a phrase for them: an army of peace. Sailors and boys climbing, vaulting, and carrying each other in front of delegates from a dozen countries, seventeen months before the other army goes north. No period account of the session was retrieved in this research, and the phrase reaches us at second hand. What is certain is that within weeks he is offered the direction of the first physical-education college in France.
suggested_refs: The 1913 International Congress of Physical Education, Paris
sources: research dossier, on the contemporary press framing

stops.name: Paris, unpaid leave and the Panhard detachment
stops.date_confidence: Date attested to the day by fr.wikipedia ('1er avril 1913, détaché en congé sans solde chez Panhard et Levassor, Paris'). The dossier framed this as a posting 'just before the outbreak of war', which is wrong by sixteen months; it is the same date as the Reims opening and is read here as the administrative mechanism behind it. The Panhard works address was not pinned, so the coordinate is central Paris.
stops.campa: On the first of April 1913 the Navy places him on unpaid leave, detached to Panhard et Levassor in Paris. The automobile firm is the shape the paperwork takes; the substance is that a serving lieutenant de vaisseau cannot run a civilian college in Champagne while he is on the books. He does not resign his commission and he draws no pay. This is not a career change and not a retirement, and the paperwork is careful to make it neither. The detachment and the opening of the college at Reims carry the same date.
suggested_refs: fr.wikipedia, 'Georges Hébert', on the congé sans solde of 1 April 1913

stops.name: Reims, technical director in the Pommery park
stops.date_confidence: Opening date 1 April 1913 from fr.wikipedia, 'Collège d'athlètes de Reims'. Coordinate is the Parc de Champagne, 49° 14′ 19″ N 4° 03′ 18″ E per fr.wikipedia, which supersedes both the dossier's 4.0483 and the afterlife lens's cathedral-area 4.0317. Unresolved contradiction: fr.wikipedia's article on the college says it was founded by Édouard Redont and that Hébert did not direct it, against en.wikipedia and both articles on Hébert, which make him technical director from April 1913.
stops.campa: In the park the Marquis de Polignac laid out between 1909 and 1911 for the workers of the Pommery cellars, twenty-one and a half hectares on the Butte Saint-Nicaise, a college of athletes opens with Hébert as its technical director. A gymnasium forty metres by twenty, an oval track, an open-air pool, boxing rings, fencing halls. Instructors are trained here, not only athletes. It is the first institution of its kind in France, and the French encyclopedia article on the college itself flatly denies that he ran it.
suggested_refs: fr.wikipedia, 'Parc de Champagne', on the Polignac park and its 1913 conversion to a sports training centre

stops.name: Reims, Poincaré inaugurates the college
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day by fr.wikipedia, 'Parc de Champagne' ('inauguré le 19 octobre 1913 par le président Raymond Poincaré'); en.wikipedia gives only 'October 1913'. Jean Bouin's October 1913 visit and four-minute filming, at Hébert's invitation, are from fr.wikipedia, 'Jean Bouin', which states he did not train there regularly and followed his own method.
stops.campa: President Raymond Poincaré comes to Reims on the nineteenth of October and inaugurates the college in front of the champagne families and the sporting press. His France is ten months from mobilization. Jean Bouin, the best distance runner in the country, visits that same month at Hébert's invitation and is filmed for four minutes moving through the grounds. He is not training there; he is visiting. He keeps to a method of his own and does not stay.
suggested_refs: The four-minute cinematographic short of Jean Bouin at the Collège d'athlètes, October 1913

stops.name: Cherbourg, the eighth company goes north
stops.date_confidence: Contradiction, unresolved. The dossier gives a departure from Cherbourg on 28 August 1914 with 249 men; fr.wikipedia dates his commission as captain of the 8th company, 2nd marine regiment, to 14 October 1914, by which point the brigade is already fighting in Belgium. fr.wikipedia, 'Brigade de fusiliers marins', confirms the brigade's creation on 7 August 1914 and Cherbourg among its ports, but does not name Hébert. Date here follows the dossier and is flagged.
stops.campa: The brigade of marine fusiliers is raised on the seventh of August, sailors turned infantry because the fleet is not going to fight and the Belgian coast is. Hébert, thirty-nine, takes the eighth company of the second regiment, two hundred and forty-nine men, and they go north out of Cherbourg. The records disagree about when: an end-of-August departure in one account, a captaincy dated the fourteenth of October in another, by which time the brigade has been in Belgium for weeks and has already lost men at Melle.
suggested_refs: fr.wikipedia, 'Brigade de fusiliers marins', for the unit's mobilization and route

stops.name: Melle, covering the Belgian retreat
stops.date_confidence: Unit-level attestation: fr.wikipedia, 'Brigade de fusiliers marins', gives the combat at Melle, 9 to 11 October 1914. That article does not name Hébert. His presence rests on his company's presence and is an inference, not a sourced individual fact.
stops.campa: Between the ninth and the eleventh of October the brigade fights at Melle, east of Ghent, holding the road while the Belgian field army pulls back westward toward the Yser. It is the first infantry action for men who were serving guns at sea eight weeks earlier, and they take it standing. The unit records the engagement and its dates. It does not record Hébert. That he was there is a reasonable inference drawn from where his company was, and it is nothing stronger than that.
suggested_refs: fr.wikipedia, 'Brigade de fusiliers marins', combat at Melle, 9-11 October 1914

stops.name: Diksmuide, the bridgehead held three weeks
stops.date_confidence: Unit-level facts attested by fr.wikipedia, 'Brigade de fusiliers marins': arrival 15 October, roughly 6,000 men in two regiments, Ronarc'h's order to hold at least four days, withdrawal across the Yser 10 November. German strength corrected downward from the dossier's 50,000 to the sourced figure of about 30,000. The quote's usual citation to Le Goffic 1915 is false: see quote_source.
stops.campa: On the fifteenth of October six thousand marine fusiliers under Admiral Ronarc'h dig in at Diksmuide on the near bank of the Yser, under an order to hold at least four days. Some thirty thousand German troops under the Duke of Württemberg come at the bridgehead. They hold it for three weeks and cross back over the river on the tenth of November with the road to Dunkirk still shut. The line the schoolbooks keep from those weeks is a line about strength, and its paper trail does not survive inspection.
stops.quote: Soyons forts ! Les faibles sont des inutiles ou des lâches !
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Hébert at Dixmude, October 1914, via fr.wikipedia. Its usual citation, Charles Le Goffic, Dixmude (Plon, 1915), pp. 89-91, is FALSE: a full-text search of the 1915 edition on archive.org returns zero hits for 'Soyons' and 'lâches', and none of its eight mentions of Hébert falls near pp. 89-91. fr.wikipedia's second reference is Jean Mabire, La Bataille de l'Yser, unverified. Treat as reconstruction.
suggested_refs: Charles Le Goffic, Dixmude (Plon, 1915), a contemporary chronicle that mentions Hébert eight times and does not contain the motto
sources: Le Goffic, Dixmude (1915), archive.org dixmudeunchapitr00legouoft, searched

stops.name: North of the bridgehead, the arm
stops.date_confidence: Contradiction, unresolved. The dossier, citing Pierre Philippe-Meden's archival reconstruction, dates the wounding to 19 October 1914 with hospitalization following in November; en.wikipedia states the wounding itself occurred in November 1914. The manual-in-the-pocket detail is dossier-only and was not independently located. Date here follows the dossier and is flagged.
stops.campa: Ordered north from the bridgehead to reinforce another company under heavy artillery, his men lose about forty. A bullet strikes him and is stopped by a manual and a notebook carried in his greatcoat pocket, paper thick enough to hold it. A second passes through his left arm. One reconstruction dates the morning to the nineteenth of October and the English encyclopedia dates it to November, and nobody has yet reconciled the two accounts. The arm never works properly again.
suggested_refs: Pierre Philippe-Meden's archival work on Hébert's war service

stops.name: Paris, admitted to the Hôpital Lariboisière
stops.date_confidence: Hospital location independently confirmed (fr.wikipedia, 'Hôpital Lariboisière'). The admission date and the clinical list come from the dossier's citation of Philippe-Meden's archival reconstruction, which was not independently opened; the permanent left-arm disability is widely attested. The intermediate stop at Calais is dossier-only and unverified.
stops.campa: Evacuated by way of Calais, he reaches the Hôpital Lariboisière in the tenth arrondissement on the twenty-third of November. The man who has told a thousand conscripts to be strong in order to be useful is carried in unable to lift his own arm. He is thirty-nine. The date and the clinical detail reach us through an archival reconstruction rather than a record opened here. The condition on admission is set down as cachexia, hospital gangrene, purulent infiltration, erysipelas, the radial nerve severed clean through, paraplegic complications.
suggested_refs: The Hôpital Lariboisière, 2 rue Ambroise-Paré, Paris 10e

segments.name: La Palestra: Women, the Journal, and the War on Sport

stops.name: Reims, the college shelled to pieces
stops.date_confidence: The destruction is attested in general terms by en.wikipedia and fr.wikipedia, 'Collège d'athlètes de Reims' ('ayant subi de grands dommages lors du conflit de 14-18'), without a date. Date here is set to 1915 to order the segment. Jean Bouin's death on 29 September 1914 at Xivray-et-Marvoisin is attested by fr.wikipedia, 'Jean Bouin'; the dossier's claim that his death ended the college's era is dropped, since Reims was already under bombardment.
stops.campa: Reims is a front-line city from September 1914 and stays one for four years. The cathedral burns. The college in the Pommery park is shelled into pieces, and instructors and athletes of that brief establishment are killed in the general slaughter; among the dead of that same autumn is Jean Bouin, hit by shrapnel at Xivray-et-Marvoisin on the twenty-ninth of September, probably by French guns. Hébert loses the institution while lying in a hospital bed in Paris with a dead arm. Thirteen months of it existed.
suggested_refs: fr.wikipedia, 'Collège d'athlètes de Reims', on the war damage and partial reconstruction

stops.name: Tourgéville, La Palestra opens
stops.date_confidence: Founding year contested: en.wikipedia gives 1918, other accounts 1919, and a 1991 federation documentary gives 1925, which is dropped as an outlier. fr.wikipedia, 'Hébertisme', dates the héberto-naturiste women's community to 'entre 1918 et 1929', supporting 1918. Coordinate corrected to Tourgéville proper (49° 19′ 26″ N 0° 03′ 53″ E per fr.wikipedia); the dossier's 49.354, 0.093 lies about 3.4 km away, effectively in Deauville. No building footprint located.
stops.campa: On the Normandy coast behind Deauville he and Yvonne Moreau open La Palestra, a residential college for women and children: outdoor natural-method training, gardening, manual work, hygiene instruction, and what the programme calls psychic gymnastics. The women live on the site. Sources give the founding as 1918 and as 1919 with equal confidence, and the difference may only be between founding a thing and beginning to run it. Which year the women first climbed there is not settled.
suggested_refs: fr.wikipedia, 'Hébertisme', on the héberto-naturiste women's community, 1918-1929

stops.name: Paris, L'Éducation physique féminine
stops.date_confidence: Year attested by three sources in agreement: en.wikipedia 'Georges Hébert', en.wikipedia 'Méthode naturelle', and the fr.wikipedia bibliography. The dossier's claimed 1921 versus 1919 disagreement between the two English articles does not exist and has been removed. Month and day unknown and defaulted; coordinate is the central Paris placeholder.
stops.campa: L'Éducation physique féminine: muscle et beauté plastique. The argument is against the corset and for the muscle it hides. A woman's body is a body; it should run, climb, throw, carry, and defend itself, and a garment that prevents this is a deformity sold as modesty. Three separate sources put the book in 1919 and, unusually in this life, agree with each other. The plates show women outdoors, unlaced, caught mid-movement rather than arranged for the camera.
suggested_refs: L'Éducation physique féminine: muscle et beauté plastique (1919)

stops.name: Paris, the journal L'Éducation physique
stops.date_confidence: Year and span attested by fr.wikipedia, 'Hébertisme': Hébert directed the journal between 1922 and 1940, eighteen years, correcting the dossier's 'roughly three decades'. The month of May is dossier-only. No editorial address was located, so the coordinate is central Paris as a placeholder.
stops.campa: He takes over L'Éducation physique, relaunches it, and directs it until 1940: eighteen years of a periodical through which the method is taught, defended, and policed. Instructors write in and he answers. Sessions, tables, photographs, polemic, month after month. A doctrine that was a way of training now has a nervous system, and for eighteen years he is the one working it. No editorial address survives in any reachable source, so this stop is pinned to the city and no closer.
suggested_refs: The review L'Éducation physique, 1922-1940, organ of Hébertism
sources: research dossier, for the May 1922 relaunch

stops.name: Paris, marriage to Yvonne Moreau
stops.date_confidence: Contradiction, unresolved. A French naval biographical register cited in the dossier gives 4 January 1923; en.wikipedia and the popular biographies give 1924. Neither was adjudicated. Date here follows the register because it is the more precise of the two. Yvonne Moreau's role as chief female instructor at Reims in 1913 is attested by en.wikipedia.
stops.campa: He marries Yvonne Marguerite Charlotte Moreau in the sixteenth arrondissement. She was trained in the Demenÿ system, was chief female instructor at the Reims college in 1913, and has been running the Palestra as its director since the war ended. He is forty-seven, or forty-eight: a naval biographical register dates the wedding to the fourth of January 1923 and the popular biographies say 1924, and nobody has reconciled the two. The register is followed here because it is the more precise of them, not because it is the better attested.
suggested_refs: The French naval biographical register entry for Hébert, cited in the research dossier
sources: research dossier, citing a naval biographical register

stops.name: Cannes, the winter Palestra
stops.date_confidence: Year and Riviera location attested by en.wikipedia ('1923: Created winter palestra on French Riviera'); no town, building, or terms were located. Coordinate is Cannes, chosen as an honest coastal anchor. The dossier's 43.65, 7.0 is described there as 'near Nice' but lies inland behind Cannes, some 22 km from Nice, and is not used.
stops.campa: A winter branch of the Palestra opens on the Riviera in 1923, moving the residential programme south for the cold months. What is documented is the pattern rather than the address: sea, air, open ground, no apparatus at all, women and children training out of doors through the months when the rest of the country trains its boys indoors. Which town, which building, and on what terms are recorded nowhere reachable. The pin here is a coastal anchor and not a site.
suggested_refs: The winter Palestra on the French Riviera, 1923, site unlocated

stops.name: Paris, against the Olympics
stops.date_confidence: en.wikipedia records the public condemnation of modern competitive sport in the wake of the 1924 Paris Olympics but supplies no occasion, venue, or text, so the item is tagged reconstruction. Date set to the month of the Games; coordinate is the central Paris placeholder.
stops.campa: The Games come to Paris and Hébert turns on the entire enterprise. Records, specialization, spectators, the athlete built lopsided by a single event and cheered for the deformity: he calls this the opposite of physical education, not a variety of it. The man who published a scoring table in 1911 now argues that scoring is the disease. He is forty-nine. From here he opposes organized sport for the rest of his life, and organized sport goes on to take the century.
suggested_refs: The 1924 Paris Olympic Games, occasion of Hébert's break with competitive sport

stops.name: Paris, Le Sport contre l'éducation physique
stops.date_confidence: Publication year and publisher (Vuibert) attested by both wikis; month and day unknown and defaulted. The definition quoted is verbatim from fr.wikipedia but carries no footnote or page number there, and the 1925 edition is not on archive.org and Gallica's SRU endpoint returned 403, so it could not be checked against the book.
stops.campa: Vuibert publishes the polemic, and its title concedes nothing: sport against physical education, the two set at each other rather than ranked. Inside it he defines the enemy exactly, as struggle undertaken for a performance, against a distance, a danger, an animal, an opponent, and finally against oneself. The definition is quoted everywhere in French and carries a page number nowhere, because the 1925 edition has never been digitized and the sentence has been handed along for a hundred years.
stops.quote: tout genre d'exercice ou d'activité physique ayant pour but la réalisation d'une performance et dont l'exécution repose essentiellement sur l'idée de lutte contre un élément défini, une distance, un danger, un animal, un adversaire [...] et par extension contre soi-même
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Le Sport contre l'éducation physique (Paris, Vuibert, 1925) by fr.wikipedia, section 'L'éducation physique et le sport', unfootnoted; the raw wikitext carries no page reference and the 1925 edition was not reachable.
suggested_refs: Le Sport contre l'éducation physique (Vuibert, 1925), not digitized

stops.name: Deauville, the schooner Alcyon
stops.date_confidence: Year contested and carried as a live discrepancy: en.wikipedia gives 1929 ('Established marine palestra aboard ship', 'Created Women's Nautical School aboard ship'), fr.wikipedia gives 1930 for the receipt of the Alcyon and the founding of the first women's nautical school aboard her. The 'and boys under 14' element is in neither wiki. Coordinate is Deauville as the Palestra's home base, not a verified mooring.
stops.campa: A three-masted schooner, the Alcyon, comes into his hands, and he founds a nautical school aboard her for girls: the Palestra put afloat. Rigging as climbing, deck work as lifting and carrying, the sea itself as the ground underfoot. The French record dates this to 1930 and the English record to 1929, and both state it flatly, and neither cites anything. Where she moored, who owned her, and what she actually did in the water are not written down anywhere now reachable.
suggested_refs: The three-masted schooner Alcyon and the women's nautical school

stops.name: Tourgéville, the break with the Groupement hébertiste
stops.date_confidence: Year from fr.wikipedia; no independent corroboration was located in this research, and no site of the announcement is known. The stop is placed at Tourgéville as his base at the time, with the corrected Tourgéville coordinate, and is tagged reconstruction.
stops.campa: A Groupement hébertiste has formed: an association, a membership, a claim on the name. Hébert separates himself from it publicly. The method was never meant to be a federation, and a federation is what happens to methods. The doctrine has escaped him in both directions at once, taken up by people he never authorized and taught in schools he has never seen. Standing off from the association is the only move a founder has left, and it changes nothing about who uses the name. He is sixty-three.
suggested_refs: The Groupement hébertiste and the institutionalization of the method

segments.name: The Summa and the Last Years

stops.name: Paris, the volumes begin
stops.date_confidence: Start year and the 1936-1959 span attested by en.wikipedia, 'Méthode naturelle', and the fr.wikipedia bibliography; individual tome and fascicle dates were not collated. Month and day unknown and defaulted; coordinate is the central Paris placeholder.
stops.campa: From 1936 the tomes and fascicles of L'Éducation physique virile et morale par la méthode naturelle start coming out. He is sixty-one when the first one appears. It is the whole system set down at length: doctrine, method, exercises, tables, plates, the argument restated for readers who were not born when it began. He works at it for the last twenty-one years of his life and does not finish it. The volumes keep appearing until 1959, two years after he is dead.
suggested_refs: L'Éducation physique virile et morale par la méthode naturelle, in tomes and fascicles, 1936-1959

stops.name: Tourgéville, the Palestra bombarded
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. en.wikipedia states the Normandy Palestra was destroyed by bombardment during the Second World War; no date, no specific action, and no photograph were located. Date set to 1944 to order the segment, consistent with the general destruction along that coast around the landings, and not attested.
stops.campa: The Normandy coast is fortified, then invaded, and the Palestra buildings are destroyed by bombardment. His wife had directed the school there for a quarter of a century. It is the second time a war has shelled an institution of his out of existence: Reims in 1914, Tourgéville somewhere between 1939 and 1945. He is in his late sixties. Which shells, on which day, and whether anything was left standing is not written down in anything located here.
suggested_refs: The destruction of La Palestra, Normandy, during the Second World War

stops.name: Tourgéville, the stroke
stops.date_confidence: Year attested by en.wikipedia ('1953: Suffered a stroke that affected his speech; had to relearn walking, speaking, and writing'); month and day unknown and defaulted. Place is his known residence, not separately sourced for the event itself.
stops.campa: At seventy-eight a stroke takes his speech. He relearns walking, then speaking, then writing, and he does it on exactly the terms he spent fifty years prescribing to other people: progression, patience, work in the order the body will accept, nothing used that the day does not already provide. He has been relearning his left arm since a bullet went through it in Belgium, so the procedure is not new to him, and neither is the idea that a damaged body is the ordinary case rather than the exception. He goes on writing the fascicles. There is no record of his remarking on any of it.
suggested_refs: The 1953 stroke and the last four years of work

stops.name: Tourgéville, Commandeur de la Légion d'honneur
stops.date_confidence: Year attested by fr.wikipedia, section 'Reconnaissance et notoriété', and en.wikipedia; month, day, and place of the award are unknown, so the stop sits at his residence and the date is defaulted. Chevalier 1911 and Officier d'académie 1914 are from the same fr.wikipedia section. The parcours du combattant attribution is tagged reconstruction in the sources.
stops.campa: Fifty years after the first cohorts at Lorient he is made Commandeur de la Légion d'honneur. He was a Chevalier in 1911 and an Officier d'académie in 1914; the higher grade arrives at eighty, from a Republic whose schools teach a physical education he has spent thirty years attacking in print. The obstacle course that every French conscript runs, the parcours du combattant, came out of his war and his method, and about that part nobody in the ministry is arguing. He accepts the ribbon.
suggested_refs: The parcours du combattant, the French military obstacle course descended from Hébert's parcours

stops.name: Tourgéville, death in Calvados
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day by fr.wikipedia and en.wikipedia on Hébert and by fr.wikipedia, 'Tourgéville'. The heart attack is movement tradition; no death certificate or medical record was located. Coordinate corrected to Tourgéville's own (49.324, 0.065); the two research lenses had given 49.354/0.093 and 49.3444/0.0917, both wrong. The closing quote is doubly secondary: see quote_source.
stops.campa: He dies at Tourgéville on the second of August 1957, aged eighty-two, in the commune where the Palestra stood. The movement remembers a heart attack; no certificate and no medical record were found to confirm it. Neither the French nor the English reference works name a cemetery, a grave, or a stone, and no one located one. What survives in place of a tomb is a distinction he drew late, in an interview, between the thing he built and the thing that got named after him.
stops.quote: The natural method is not Hébertism, and it should not be called so... Hébertism is something else... it is the philosophy that must emerge from this natural method to encourage the individual to put at the service of others what he can derive from his physical and virile training.
stops.quote_source: Hébert quoted by Marcel Defarges, revue L'Éducation physique, 2e trimestre 1958, p. 55, via the hebertisme.com FAQ page cited by en.wikipedia. That page no longer resolves and the archives were unreachable, so the words were seen only in Wikipedia's blockquote. Two layers of secondary handling.
suggested_refs: Marcel Defarges's posthumous interview transcript, revue L'Éducation physique, 2e trimestre 1958

stops.name: Deauville, Yvonne outlives the work
stops.date_confidence: Yvonne Moreau Hébert's death year attested by en.wikipedia; month, day, and place unknown, so the stop is pinned at Deauville and the date defaulted. The two named facilities, the Deauville municipal stadium and a sports complex in northern Reims, are from fr.wikipedia, section 'Reconnaissance et notoriété', and are tagged reconstruction there.
stops.campa: Yvonne Moreau Hébert dies in 1975, eighteen years after her husband, having outlasted the Reims college, two wars, and the bombardment of the school she directed. The municipal stadium at Deauville carries his name; so does a sports complex in the north of Reims. Two named grounds are the whole of the monumental record, in a country whose obstacle courses still carry his name. No statue was found, no grave was located, and no plaque has been photographed for any reference work consulted here.
suggested_refs: The stade Georges-Hébert at Deauville and the sports complex at Reims

stops.name: Reims, the ground becomes a public park
stops.date_confidence: Undated in sources. The partial post-1918 reconstruction, chiefly a swimming pool and a diving board, and the architects Édouard Redont and Ernest Kalas, are from fr.wikipedia, 'Collège d'athlètes de Reims' and 'Parc de Champagne'; the renaming of the parc des sports Pommery to the parc de Champagne carries no date there. The date here orders the segment and asserts nothing.
stops.campa: The Pommery sports park is rebuilt only in part after 1918, and by architects, Édouard Redont and Ernest Kalas, whose names later attach themselves to the founding of the college and confuse the record permanently. A swimming pool goes back up, and a diving board. The rest does not. The first physical-education college in France stood on this ground for thirteen months. The twenty-one hectares are municipal now, open to anyone, and called the Parc de Champagne.
suggested_refs: fr.wikipedia, 'Parc de Champagne', 21.6 hectares, formerly the parc des sports Pommery

stops.name: Tourgéville, the method comes back in English
stops.date_confidence: Til's 2014 translation, the 1912 Pilou and Gregg translation, Le Corre's MovNat, and the credited influence on parkour through David Belle, on Sébastien Foucan's freerunning, and on John-Edouard Ehlinger are all from en.wikipedia, 'Georges Hébert'. Raymond Belle's transmission of the method through the French military is the QUEUE.md framing and is not documented as personal contact with Hébert. movnat.com returned 404 on fetch. Stop is pinned at Tourgéville and dated to Til's edition to order the segment.
stops.campa: The parcours Hébert stays alive in French as the ordinary name for an outdoor obstacle course, in towns that have forgotten whose name it is. Philippe Til translates the manuals into English in 2014, a century late; an earlier translation by Pilou and Gregg had appeared in 1912 and disappeared. Erwan Le Corre builds MovNat out of the method and sells it. And the parcours becomes parkour: Raymond Belle trained in the méthode naturelle through the French military, and his son David made a discipline of it.
suggested_refs: Georges Hébert, trans. Philippe Til, The Natural Method: Georges Hébert's Practical Guide to Physical Education, vol. 1 (2014)
